new_statements.quote: [p.88, quoting Hayward & Chabo 2014:55] Like some other languages of the Horn, Gamo is best described as a 'tonal-accent language', in which a very simple tonal melody is mapped onto a string of tone-bearing elements (syllables / morae) belonging to a particular structure (the tone phrase), aided sometimes by an accentual diacritic. [p.95, Thomassen] Most of the words that were uttered in isolation do in fact have one syllable whose pitch is higher than the other syllable(s) of the word. This higher pitch is taken to be the manifestation of high tone. [p.93] The Bonke variety of Gamo is a simple tone system, and the notion of tonal accent is not necessary to explain this system.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source describes dynamic word stress; prominence is a single High tone. Hayward 1994 / Hayward & Chabo 2014 (reported by Thomassen pp. 86-90): one H per tone phrase, realised on the first word; it docks on a lexically accented root mora/syllable, otherwise by default on the ultimate stem syllable of nouns and adjectives (Hayward 1994: the terminal vowel) and on the first post-thematic syllable of verbs; a word in isolation is its own phrase so every citation form has exactly one H. Thomassen's own Bonke data: most isolated words have one H syllable, in any position (first, middle, last), but she finds final contour tones, all-L words and double-H words and reanalyses the variety as an H/L tone language with the syllable as TBU.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned. Hayward & Chabo (via Thomassen p. 89) describe automatic rightward H spreading over one or two morae within the phrasal word, never onto a word-final mora in a one-word phrase.
new_statements.exceptions: Per Hayward & Chabo (via Thomassen pp. 89, 94): a few items with lexical H on several morae (names, ébéló 'so-and-so', issínó 'one'); passive stems accented, causative stems unaccented; verbal noun in -o always H on root; plural suffix attracts H in TV-accented nouns (duuná > duunatí); definite suffix treated as clitic; no H on 2nd mora of a word-final long vowel. Thomassen: modified head nouns surface without H (sec. 6.4.3); contour tones on final syllables (moiâô 'lip').
new_statements.domain_note: Hayward: domain of H is the phonological/tone phrase (first word only carries H); statements about citation forms follow because an isolated word = one phrase. Thomassen's data are isolated words and short NPs from Bonke wereda speakers; Hayward & Chabo describe the Chencha-area variety (Thomassen p. 117).
new_statements.identity_note: Thomassen 2015 describes the Bonke wereda variety of Gamo (speakers from Gazzeso, Laakka Godda, Zalla Dolla); Hayward 1994 and Hayward & Chabo 2014 describe the Chencha-area variety (Thomassen p. 117). Glottolog 5.1 lists no sub-dialect codes under gamo1243; Kole (Samuel 2016) and Ochollo theses are also filed under gamo1243. All sources agree prominence is tonal (single H), differing only on tonal-accent vs. H/L-tone analysis; none describes dynamic stress.
